title: Surface, Living and Radiological Anatomy (ANA 411)
description: Surface landmarks and projections of viscera and vessels, clinical procedures based on surface anatomy, and normal radiological anatomy on plain films, CT and ultrasound.

topics.title: Surface Anatomy of the Thorax
topics.summary: Bony landmarks, projections of the lungs, pleura and heart, and valve auscultation areas.

notes.b: Key landmarks: the jugular (suprasternal) notch (T2/T3), sternal angle (2nd costal cartilage, T4/T5 — used to count ribs), xiphisternal joint (T9), the nipple in males (4th intercostal space), and the inferior angle of the scapula (7th rib/T7 with arms by the side). The lung apices rise about 2.5 cm above the medial third of the clavicle (at risk in neck injuries and subclavian cannulation). The lower lung borders lie at the 6th rib in the midclavicular line, 8th in the midaxillary line and 10th at the vertebral column; the pleura extends two ribs lower (8th, 10th, 12th), forming the costodiaphragmatic recess. The oblique fissure follows the line of the 5th/6th rib from T3 posteriorly; the horizontal fissure (right) runs along the 4th costal cartilage.

The heart's borders project from the 3rd right costal cartilage to the 6th right costal cartilage (right border), to the apex at the left 5th intercostal space in the midclavicular line, and up to the 2nd left costal cartilage. Auscultation areas differ from anatomical valve positions: aortic (right 2nd ICS parasternal), pulmonary (left 2nd ICS), tricuspid (left lower sternal edge, 4th/5th ICS), mitral (apex). Clinical procedures: needle decompression of tension pneumothorax (2nd ICS midclavicular line or 4th/5th ICS anterior axillary line), chest drain insertion in the 'triangle of safety' (anterior border of latissimus dorsi, lateral border of pectoralis major, line of the 5th ICS, apex below the axilla), and pericardiocentesis (subxiphoid).
k: Triangle of safety for chest drains
Needle decompression: 2nd ICS MCL or 4th/5th ICS AAL

topics.title: Surface Anatomy of the Abdomen and Pelvis
topics.summary: Abdominal planes and regions, surface markings of organs, and clinical landmarks.

notes.b: The transpyloric plane (of Addison) lies halfway between the jugular notch and the pubic symphysis, at L1: it passes through the pylorus, fundus of the gallbladder (at the 9th costal cartilage), neck of the pancreas, duodenojejunal flexure, hila of the kidneys and origin of the superior mesenteric artery; the spinal cord ends near this level in adults. The subcostal plane is at L3; the umbilicus at L3/L4 (variable); the supracristal (intercristal) plane at L4 — used to locate the L4 spinous process for lumbar puncture; the transtubercular plane at L5. The abdomen is divided into nine regions by two vertical midclavicular lines and the subcostal and transtubercular planes, or into four quadrants.

The liver lies mainly in the right hypochondrium, its lower border along the right costal margin; the spleen lies along the left 9th–11th ribs, its long axis along the 10th rib — a normal spleen is not palpable and enlarges towards the right iliac fossa. The kidneys lie at T12–L3, the right slightly lower than the left. McBurney's point (appendix base) is one-third of the way from the anterior superior iliac spine to the umbilicus. The mid-inguinal point (halfway between ASIS and pubic symphysis) marks the femoral artery pulse; the deep inguinal ring lies just above the midpoint of the inguinal ligament. Suprapubic catheterisation is performed in the midline just above the pubic symphysis with a full bladder.

topics.title: Surface Anatomy of the Limbs and Clinical Procedures
topics.summary: Pulses, nerves at risk, veins for cannulation, and safe injection sites.

notes.b: Palpable pulses: radial (lateral to flexor carpi radialis tendon at the wrist), ulnar, brachial (medial to the biceps tendon in the cubital fossa — used for BP measurement and in infants for CPR pulse check), axillary, femoral (mid-inguinal point), popliteal (deep in the popliteal fossa with knee flexed), posterior tibial (behind the medial malleolus, between it and the calcaneus) and dorsalis pedis (lateral to the extensor hallucis longus tendon on the dorsum of the foot). Nerves at risk: the ulnar nerve behind the medial epicondyle ('funny bone'), the common fibular nerve at the neck of the fibula, the radial nerve in the spiral groove, and the median nerve at the wrist.
k: Common fibular nerve at fibular neck

notes.b: Veins commonly used for venepuncture and cannulation: median cubital vein (cubital fossa — connects cephalic and basilic veins; median nerve and brachial artery lie deep to the bicipital aponeurosis), cephalic vein (anatomical snuffbox, lateral forearm — the 'houseman's vein'), dorsal venous network of the hand, and the great saphenous vein anterior to the medial malleolus (used for venous cutdown and in coronary bypass grafts). Intramuscular injection sites: deltoid (2–3 finger-breadths below the acromion, to avoid the axillary nerve), ventrogluteal (gluteus medius — safest in adults), vastus lateralis (middle third of the anterolateral thigh — preferred in infants), and the upper outer quadrant of the buttock (dorsogluteal — risk of sciatic nerve injury if placed wrongly).
k: Great saphenous vein anterior to medial malleolus

topics.title: Radiological Anatomy: Plain Radiographs
topics.summary: Normal anatomy on chest, abdominal and skeletal radiographs.

notes.b: On a PA chest radiograph: the trachea is central; the right heart border is formed by the right atrium; the left heart border by the aortic knuckle (arch), pulmonary trunk, left auricle and left ventricle; the right hemidiaphragm is usually slightly higher than the left (liver); costophrenic angles are sharp; the hila contain the pulmonary arteries and main bronchi (the left hilum is usually slightly higher). Silhouette sign: loss of a normal border indicates adjacent pathology (e.g. loss of the right heart border — right middle lobe consolidation; loss of the left heart border — lingular disease; loss of the hemidiaphragm — lower lobe disease). Normal gastric air bubble lies under the left hemidiaphragm.
k: Left border: aortic knuckle, pulmonary trunk, left ventricle

notes.b: On an abdominal radiograph, small bowel lies centrally with valvulae conniventes crossing the whole width; large bowel lies peripherally with haustra that do not cross the full width; normal diameters — small bowel < 3 cm, colon < 6 cm, caecum < 9 cm ('3-6-9 rule'). Psoas shadows, kidney outlines and bones are assessed. Skeletal radiographs: in children, growth plates (physes) and secondary ossification centres must not be mistaken for fractures — the elbow ossification centres appear in order CRITOE (capitulum, radial head, internal/medial epicondyle, trochlea, olecranon, external/lateral epicondyle) at roughly 1, 3, 5, 7, 9 and 11 years. Bone age from hand radiographs assesses growth.

topics.title: Cross-sectional Anatomy: CT, MRI and Ultrasound
topics.summary: Orientation conventions, normal anatomy on axial CT of the head, chest and abdomen, and ultrasound basics.

notes.b: Axial CT and MRI images are viewed as if looking up from the patient's feet: the patient's right is on the viewer's left, and anterior is at the top. CT densities (Hounsfield units): air −1,000, fat about −100, water 0, soft tissue +20 to +80, acute blood +50 to +80, bone +400 to +1,000. On non-contrast head CT: grey matter slightly denser than white matter, CSF dark in ventricles and sulci, acute haemorrhage bright (hyperdense), acute infarct becomes dark (hypodense) over hours. On abdominal CT at the level of the kidneys: liver (right), spleen (left), aorta (left of midline, anterior to the vertebra), IVC (right of the aorta), pancreas crossing anterior to the aorta, and kidneys in the retroperitoneum.
k: Aorta left of midline; IVC right

notes.b: MRI uses magnetic fields and radiofrequency pulses without ionising radiation: on T1-weighted images fat is bright and water/CSF dark (good anatomy); on T2-weighted images water/CSF and oedema are bright (good pathology). MRI excels for brain, spinal cord, soft tissues, ligaments and joints; contraindications include some pacemakers, ferromagnetic implants and metallic foreign bodies in the eye. Ultrasound uses high-frequency sound: fluid is anechoic (black), with posterior acoustic enhancement; stones and bone cause bright echoes with posterior acoustic shadowing; air blocks ultrasound. It is ideal for obstetrics, gallbladder, liver, kidneys, pelvis and vessels (Doppler), and FAST scanning in trauma. Higher-frequency probes give better resolution but less penetration.
k: T1: fat bright; T2: water bright
High frequency: better resolution, less penetration
